text: Chapter 3 has mentioned tax lines several times without stopping on them. This closing lesson does that, at the level a Payables user actually needs - not deep tax configuration, just enough to recognize what's happening on an invoice and why a tax amount shows up the way it does.

Transaction tax isn't calculated by logic built into Payables itself. It's calculated by Oracle Fusion Tax, a shared engine used across Payables, Receivables, and other modules, based on the invoice's details and whatever tax configuration is set up. Standard invoices, prepayments, credit memos, debit memos, and expense reports all run through this same shared engine.

A tax determinant is a piece of information - ship-from and ship-to locations, product category, the parties involved - that the tax engine uses to figure out which tax applies and at what rate. These default in automatically from the supplier, item, and business unit, but a Payables user can review and override them. Tax calculates automatically during validation, or on demand.

Self-assessed tax is a special case: the supplier doesn't charge tax, but Brightfield itself legally owes it. The invoice total doesn't change - the supplier still gets paid exactly what they billed - but Payables calculates the tax internally and creates offsetting distributions to record the liability without inflating the supplier payment. Don't confuse this with withholding tax, which is a completely different thing withheld from the supplier's payment itself, covered in Chapter 5.

Take a thousand-dollar invoice from Solara Packaging with an 8% sales tax determinant: an eighty-dollar tax line gets added, the invoice totals $1,080, and Solara gets paid the full amount. In a self-assessed scenario instead, Solara would still get paid exactly $1,000, with that $80 recorded as a liability Brightfield owes directly to the tax authority. That closes Chapter 3. Up next, Chapter 4: Validation, Holds and Approvals, starting with invoice validation itself.
